To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV-seropositivity in pregnancy is associated with lower levels of measles immunity in both mother and infant and that foreign-born mothers are more likely to have higher levels of measles immunity.
HIV infection is associated with a lower antibody response to measles vaccine in pregnant women and cord serum of their infants.
HIV-infected women and women from the United States are more likely to have inadequate levels of antibody to measles, and that the levels decline rapidly in infants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epidemiologic factors that may contribute to the decline in immunity to measles in HIV-seropositives and HIV-exposed infants.
the impact of maternal HIV infection and place of birth on the acquisition of protective immunity to measles by the fetus.
the impact of HIV and place of birth on maternal antibody levels to measles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the measles vaccine is not effective in HIV-infected pregnant mothers, but that it is effective in HIV-exposed infants, and that the vaccine is effective for all mothers and infants born outside of the United States.
HIV-seropositivity and U.S.-born status are associated with lower antibody levels and a greater risk of nonprotective immunity to measles in both pregnant women and their newborns.
the HIV-seropositivity status of a woman, her place of birth, and her CD4 count are all important factors in determining her and her infant's measles immunity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we need to be concerned that HIV-seropositivity, U.S. birth, and low CD4 count are associated with lower measles antibody levels and that these factors may increase susceptibility to measles infection.
the HIV-seronegatives and seropositives in our inner city clinic have a higher prevalence of low levels of measles antibody than those in our clinic from foreign countries.
HIV infection in pregnant women and in their infants is associated with a significant decline in antibody levels to measles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune system of HIV-seroposive pregnant women is impaired, and that HIV-seroposite mothers are at risk for not passing adequate immunity to measles to their newborn infants.
measles immunity is low in pregnant women with HIV and in their infants, and that measles immunity in infants declines rapidly.
the measles vaccine is not as effective at protecting infants born to HIV-infected women as it is in protecting infants born to uninfected women.
